paras: The stoning of the Sheppard home was an attack in June 1919 by about fifty white men and boys on the newly bought bungalow of Mr. and Mrs. B. F. Sheppard at 6718 Calumet avenue in Chicago, Illinois. The crowd broke every window in the house, and a second stoning followed about ten days later, when shots were fired at the attackers. Chicago's Black weeklies covered it as an attack the police had failed to stop and as a case of a family that refused to be driven out.

The Sheppards had lived on Woodlawn avenue for 18 years and were described by the Chicago Defender as old settlers, "highly respected" by all who knew them. According to the Chicago Whip, Benjamin Sheppard bought the bungalow a few weeks before from the firm of Depriest & Depriest.

The family moved into the house on a Wednesday, apparently June 4, 1919, and soon afterward a crowd of "fifty men and boys, all white," stormed it with bricks and stones until every window, front and back, was knocked out. The Defender put the damage at $500. It said the Grand Crossing police were called within five minutes of the start but did not arrive until 12 o'clock, by which time the house was "a wreck," although a police lieutenant lived four doors away.

On a Saturday night before June 21, probably June 14, the house was stoned again. This time two shots were fired at the fleeing attackers, and the Defender reported that it was not known whether any were hit.

After the first attack the Sheppards said that the action of the whites would not drive them from their home and that they were more determined than ever to stay. After the second, a special guard was placed around the house, and the Whip credited "Hon. Wm. Riley" with arranging bomb insurance on it. No report of an arrest or of police action against the attackers appears in the coverage.

The Chicago Defender ran the first report on its front page on June 7, 1919, under the headlines "Home Is Stormed With Brickbats" and "Police Sleep While Rowdies Stage Battle With Bricks." Its account aimed much of its criticism at the police, suggesting that "every policeman at the Grand Crossing station was fast asleep," and under the subhead "Bombarders Lower Class" it described the neighborhood as people not up to standard "either in intelligence or prosperity." The second attack drew only a short item on page 16 of the June 21 Defender, headed "Marauders Still Active," which noted that Sheppard "has all the latest implements."

The Chicago Whip told the story on its front page on June 24 as "Thugs Make a Second Attack on Prominent Citizen's Home," with the subhead "Received With Bullets on Last Visit." Writing in an ironic tone, the Whip said the "modern Klu Klux Klan" had given the family a "reception" of rocks and that on the second visit the household returned "the kindness by serving them some hot lead."

The later Defender item gives the address as 6518 Calumet avenue, while the first Defender report and the Whip both give 6718. The Defender implies the attack came as the family moved in, while the Whip places it "a few days after"; the Whip also once names the householder who fired as "Mr. Smith" in a story otherwise about Sheppard.

reader.title: Stoning of the Sheppard home, Chicago
bases: A crowd of about fifty white men and boys stoned a Black family's newly bought house until every window was broken, and the house was stoned again about two weeks later (A2, A3, A4).
Two separate Black weeklies, the Chicago Defender (A2, A3) and the Chicago Whip (A4), independently report the stoning of Sheppard's bungalow on Calumet avenue and a second attack.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender report
accounts.gist: Fifty white men and boys stoned the Sheppards' new bungalow until every window was out; the Grand Crossing police, notified within minutes, came only after the house was wrecked. A later item says the house was stoned again and shots were fired at the fleeing attackers.

accounts.label: Chicago Whip report
accounts.gist: A few days after Sheppard moved in, the "modern Klu Klux Klan" threw rocks and broke windows; on the second visit they were met with "hot lead", and bomb insurance was placed on the house.

framing.detail: The Defender ran it on page one as "Police Sleep While Rowdies Stage Battle With Bricks", with a subhead "Bombarders Lower Class", praising the Sheppards as "highly respected" old settlers.

The Whip headlined "Thugs Make a Second Attack on Prominent Citizen's Home" and "Received With Bullets on Last Visit", calling the attackers the "modern Klu Klux Klan" in an ironic, approving account of armed defense.

conflicts.note: Two reports, from both papers, give 6718; the 6518 in the brief later item is likely a misprint.
The Defender's garbled text also mentions police at the house until "Tuesday morning"; the exact night is not clear.

versions.value: Sheppard ("Mr. Sheppard says he has all the latest implements")

conflicts.note: The Whip's story is about Benjamin Sheppard throughout; "Mr. Smith" appears to be an error.
